content.text:
**Probably not as the single “primary” energy source everywhere — but nuclear should be a major part of many future clean-energy systems.**

A good future grid is likely to be **diversified**: lots of wind and solar where they are cheap and abundant, backed by storage, transmission, demand response, hydro/geothermal where available, and **nuclear for firm low-carbon power** in places that can build and operate it well.

### Why nuclear deserves a big role

**1. It is low-carbon and reliable.**  
Nuclear plants produce very low operational emissions and can run day and night, independent of weather. The IEA describes nuclear as “available on demand” and useful for complementing wind and solar in net-zero electricity systems. ([iea.org](https://www.iea.org/energy-system/electricity/nuclear-power?utm_source=openai))

**2. It reduces the need for massive storage and overbuilding.**  
A grid dominated by variable renewables needs storage, transmission, backup generation, and demand flexibility. Nuclear can supply steady “firm” clean power, which can make deep decarbonization easier in some regions.

**3. It has high energy density and small land footprint.**  
Nuclear produces large amounts of electricity from comparatively small fuel and land requirements, which matters for dense countries, industrial hubs, and places with limited renewable resources.

**4. Existing nuclear plants are especially valuable.**  
Keeping safe existing reactors online is often one of the fastest ways to preserve large amounts of carbon-free electricity. The IEA has warned that losing nuclear capacity can make clean-energy transitions more difficult and expensive. ([iea.org](https://www.iea.org/reports/nuclear-power-in-a-clean-energy-system?kref=QOWNqTgorKXc&kuid=0b98f9c5-7c69-4078-a0eb-1dc5e977a00d-1736671521&utm_source=openai))

### Why it probably should not be the main source everywhere

**1. New nuclear is often expensive and slow to build.**  
Recent cost analyses still generally find new wind and solar to be cheaper than new-build nuclear in many markets. Lazard’s 2025 LCOE+ report says renewables remain the most cost-competitive form of new-build generation on an unsubsidized basis. ([lazard.com](https://www.lazard.com/research-insights/levelized-cost-of-energyplus?trk=public_post_comment-text&utm_source=openai))

**2. Construction risk is real.**  
Large nuclear projects can suffer from delays, cost overruns, financing problems, and regulatory complexity. That makes them harder to scale quickly than modular renewables, especially in countries without strong nuclear institutions.

**3. Waste and public trust remain unresolved politically, even if technically manageable.**  
The volume of nuclear waste is relatively small and can be managed through storage, reprocessing, or geological disposal, but long-term repository siting remains politically difficult in many countries. The World Nuclear Association argues waste is manageable, while critics note that many countries still lack operating final repositories for spent fuel. ([world-nuclear.org](https://world-nuclear.org/nuclear-essentials/what-is-nuclear-waste-and-what-do-we-do-with-it?utm_source=openai))

**4. Nuclear is not equally suitable for every country.**  
It requires strong regulation, technical expertise, security culture, stable institutions, emergency planning, and long-term financing. Some countries are better served prioritizing renewables, storage, grids, and efficiency.

### My view

**Nuclear should be a major pillar, not the universal primary source.** The best strategy is:

- **Keep existing safe nuclear plants running** where economically and technically feasible.
- **Build new nuclear selectively** in countries that can deliver projects on time and need firm clean power.
- **Invest in advanced reactors and SMRs**, but don’t assume they will solve cost and deployment problems until proven at scale.
- **Let renewables dominate new capacity where they are cheapest**, while using nuclear, hydro, geothermal, storage, and transmission to maintain reliability.
- **Avoid ideology**: the goal should be clean, reliable, affordable energy — not loyalty to one technology.

So, if “primary” means **the largest single source globally**, I’d say **no, probably renewables should supply the largest share**. If “primary” means **one of the core foundations of a decarbonized energy system**, then **yes, nuclear should absolutely be part of the future mix**.
